1:
The chapter opens on a king coming home from a battle he had no business fighting, and the witnesses read his safe return as at once a mercy and a rebuke waiting to fall. The reformed John Gill fixes the plain circumstance: Jehoshaphat returned from Ramoth-gilead after Ahab was slain, back to his own house at Jerusalem. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears a pointed contrast in the words “in peace”: Jehoshaphat came back whole, sound, and unhurt, where his ally lay dead on the field, and the very phrasing is set against the fate of Ahab told at 2 Chronicles 18:34.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sketches the shape of the whole chapter before dwelling on the opening clause. Jehoshaphat, on his return from Ramoth-gilead, is met by the prophet Jehu and reproved, and then goes on to make a further reformation in the land, establishing courts of justice and charging the judges and Levites to do judgment in the fear of God. “Returned in peace,” Clarke glosses, means returned in safety, notwithstanding a danger so imminent that only the especial mercy of God could have brought him out of it alive.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the bare notice into a meditation on distinguishing mercy. Here, he says, is the great favour God showed Jehoshaphat in bringing him back safe from a dangerous expedition that had nearly cost him dear. He fared better than he had expected, having been in imminent peril and yet come home in peace — and whenever we return in peace to our houses we ought to acknowledge God’s providence in preserving our going out and our coming in, and the more so when we have been kept through more than ordinary dangers, for there was but a step between us and death. He fared better than he deserved, being out of the way of his duty on an errand he could ill account for to God and his conscience, and yet returning unharmed; for God is not extreme to mark what we do amiss. And he fared better than Ahab, who was brought home slain: though Jehoshaphat had said to the king of Israel “I am as thou art” at 2 Chronicles 18:3, God distinguished between them, for he knows and owns the way of the righteous while the way of the ungodly shall perish, as Psalm 1:6 declares. Two kings had gone out together to the same field, one taken and the other left, one carried home in blood and the other in peace. Such distinguishing mercies, Henry insists, are very obliging — and they are the ground on which the prophet’s coming reproof will land, for the God who spared the king now loves him too well to leave his sin unnamed.
2:
No sooner is the king within his gates than a prophet is there to meet him. The reformed John Gill identifies the messenger and marks the courage of his lineage: Jehu was the son of that Hanani who had reproved Asa, and was put in prison for his plain dealing — yet the imprisonment of the father did not deter the son from reproving another king of Judah. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fills in the seer’s record: his father had suffered for rebuking Asa at 2 Chronicles 16:7-10, and Jehu himself had already witnessed against Baasha king of Israel at 1 Kings 16:1-7. That he went “to meet him” means he came straight into the royal presence; and Ellicott observes that the prophets never shrank from facing the highest representatives of earthly power, as Elijah had confronted Ahab at 1 Kings 21:20.

On the wording of the rebuke Ellicott is exact. “Shouldest thou help the ungodly” is in the Hebrew an infinitive — oughtest thou to help — and “the ungodly” is the emphatic word, the wicked whom the psalmist beheld with loathing at Psalm 139:21-22. The clause “therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD” repeats a phrase used at 1 Chronicles 27:24; and Ellicott asks what form that wrath took. In David’s case it was embodied in pestilence — with Jehoshaphat, he answers, the following chapters supply the reply: his land suffered invasion, his fleet was wrecked, and his posterity proved evil and came to an evil end, as the sequel at 2 Chronicles 20 begins to show; there may be a reference too to the failure of the very campaign from which he had just returned.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press both the guilt and its consequences. Adam Clarke, who had met this prophet before at 1 Kings 16:7, reads “therefore is wrath upon thee” as meaning simply, thou deservest to be punished — and he widens the warning to every age: the wrath of God rests upon all those alliances his people form with the ungodly, whether social, matrimonial, commercial, or political. John Wesley traces the chastisement through Jehoshaphat’s house: God punished the miscarriage partly by stirring up the Moabites and others to invade him at 2 Chronicles 20:1, partly by permitting his eldest son Jehoram to slay all his brethren at 2 Chronicles 21:4, and chiefly by the almost general destruction that fell upon his grandchildren at the hand of Jehu at 2 Kings 10:13-14 — all of it the bitter fruit of his affinity with Ahab. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the rebuke where it belongs in the story, as the turn that sends the chastened king back from his meddling in Israel to the work of reform at home. The witnesses do not divide: the alliance was sin, the wrath is real, and the mercy that spared the king is now the mercy that will not spare his fault.
3:
The prophet’s word does not end in condemnation, and the witnesses fasten on the “nevertheless” that turns the rebuke toward hope. The reformed John Gill reads the “good things found in thee” as the inward graces from which good works spring — principles of grace, righteousness, and holiness, of faith, love, and zeal, all true and genuine, and therefore owned by God even in a man he is chastening. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the clause a real reprieve: the divine wrath will not pursue Jehoshaphat to destruction, precisely because good things are found in him, a mercy he sets beside the like verdict on Judah at 2 Chronicles 12:12 and on the one good soul in Jeroboam’s house at 1 Kings 14:13.

Ellicott then weighs the two good things the prophet names. “Thou hast taken away the groves” he renders more sharply, “thou hast consumed,” or exterminated, the Asherahs — the sacred poles whose very name recurs elsewhere only at 2 Chronicles 33:3 and Judges 3:7, and whose destruction stood among the reforms of the faithful kings, as at 2 Kings 23:24. The second, “hast prepared thine heart to seek God,” he glosses as having directed or fixed the heart Godward — the very thing that had been denied of Rehoboam, of whom it was written that he prepared not his heart to seek the LORD at 2 Chronicles 12:14. The praise, then, is not vague: it points to a definite work of reformation already done and a settled bent of the will already formed.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the balance between the fault and the favour. The good things are good marks proceeding from an honest heart, which God more regards than this particular error of the alliance with Ahab; and therefore, though he will chasten Jehoshaphat, he will not utterly destroy him. The witnesses do not divide, and together they teach the manner of God’s dealing with his own. He does not flatter the king’s sin nor cancel the coming discipline, yet neither does he forget the graces he himself has planted. It is the pattern of a faithful reproof, Gill and Wesley agree — to name the evil plainly and yet to own the good, so that the man is neither driven to despair by the wrath nor lulled into carelessness by the mercy. The abolished groves and the prepared heart are set on the scale against the one great misstep, and the God who reads the heart finds reason, even in the midst of a rebuke, to spare.
4:
Reproved and restored, the king settles to his true work, and the witnesses read his going out among the people as the fruit of a repentance that would repair what his folly had endangered. The reformed John Gill notes the change of course: Jehoshaphat dwelt at Jerusalem and went out no more to Samaria, no longer meddling in the affairs of Israel but attending to his own. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch bind the two clauses together — when Jehoshaphat sat in Jerusalem after the war, he again went forth among the people, from Beersheba the southern frontier, named at 1 Chronicles 21:2, to Mount Ephraim the northern frontier of his kingdom, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the geography as a quiet register of the divided kingdom: before the ten tribes broke away the land was measured “from Dan to Beersheba,” but now Judah was bounded on the south by Beersheba and on the north by the mountains of Ephraim, and Jehoshaphat traversed the whole of it to examine for himself that judgment and justice were rightly administered. John Wesley reads the same circuit through the whole kingdom, its two named bounds marking its length, and explains the recovery: such as had revolted from God to idols the king reclaimed by his own counsel and example, and by the instructions of the Levites and priests he carried with him. Many, Wesley supposes, had been emboldened to idolatry when they saw their reforming king grown so intimate with idolaters; and so he thought himself doubly obliged to do all he could to restore them — for if we truly repent of sin, we shall do our utmost to repair the damage we have done to religion and to the souls of others.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott ties the progress back to the earlier commission for teaching the Law at 2 Chronicles 17:7-9, and reads “brought them back” as “made them return,” the same expression used at 2 Chronicles 24:19 — a turning of the people from the worship of the Baals and the corrupt cultus of Jehovah that, as he shows from later scholarship, had a way of fusing the two into one debased religion. Here a small difference opens among the witnesses. Clarke and Wesley picture the king himself going up and down his realm in person, examining everything with his own eyes; Ellicott cautions that “he went out” need not mean personally, but may denote the work of his accredited representatives, the commissioners through whom the visitation was conducted. The point is slight, and it does not touch the substance on which all agree: whether by the king’s own feet or by his officers, the whole land from Beersheba to Ephraim was gone over, and a people that had drifted toward the calves and the Baals was led back to the God of their fathers.
5:
With the people turned back to God, the king turns to the machinery of justice, and the witnesses see in the appointment of local judges a wise sequel to the earlier mission of teaching. The reformed John Gill explains the arrangement: these were inferior judges set in lesser courts than the great tribunal at Jerusalem, one bench in every fenced city, that judgment and justice might be executed everywhere; such courts had been ordained by David but had fallen into neglect, and Jehoshaphat now restored them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the measure as the crown of the king’s care for his people. Having done what he could to make them good by sending preachers among them to instruct them, as at 2 Chronicles 17:7-9, he now saw it further needful to send judges among them, to see the laws put in execution and to be a terror to evil-doers. There had probably been judges up and down the country before, Henry allows, but either they had neglected their business or the people had slighted them, so that the institution needed to be new-modelled, new men employed, and a fresh charge given.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the strategy of the placement: the judges were set in the fenced cities because these, as the larger towns, were the centres of communication for their neighbourhoods and so the fittest seats for a court — the phrase “city by city” answering exactly to the law’s requirement of judges “in all thy gates” at Deuteronomy 16:18. And they mark how the king laid the work upon the conscience of every judge, in words the next verse will record: not for men were they to judge, but for the LORD. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, confirms the reading — “he set” means he appointed or stationed them, the fenced cities being the chief centres of each district — and adds, from the parallel with the capital, that these provincial judges would have been Levites, and probably also priests and heads of families, as was expressly the case at Jerusalem in v.8.

The witnesses do not divide; they divide the labour of exposition. Gill fixes the courts as David’s ordinance revived; Henry sets them in the sequence of the reign, judges following preachers as execution follows instruction; Keil and Ellicott secure the sense of the terms and the law behind them. Between them they show a king who understood that a people is not kept good by teaching alone, but by teaching upheld with justice — the word of God expounded in every city by its priests, and enforced in every city by its judges, so that the reformation just carried from Beersheba to Ephraim should not be left without the settled magistracy that could preserve it.
6:
The charge to the judges is the theological heart of the chapter, and the witnesses gather around the astonishing claim it makes for the office of a magistrate. The reformed John Gill hears in “Take heed what ye do” a demand for righteous judgment strictly according to the law of God, without partiality and without respect of persons. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls it a very solemn and very necessary caution: judges should feel themselves in the place of God, and should judge as men who know that they will themselves be judged for their judgments. The weight of the warning lies in the reason attached to it — “ye judge not for man, but for the LORD.”

The grammatical-historical witnesses press that reason to its ground. Keil and Delitzsch read the words as meaning that the judges act not on the appointment or according to the will of men but in the name and according to the will of the LORD, to whom judgment belongs, as the law itself teaches at Deuteronomy 1:17 and the proverb at Proverbs 16:11. Charles Ellicott sharpens it: the judges are Jehovah’s vicegerents and the ministers of his will, in the sense the apostle gives to all lawful authority at Romans 13:1-4; and the clause “who is with you in the judgment” means that Jehovah is present with them at the very moment of giving sentence, as the psalm pictures God standing in the divine assembly to judge among the judges at Psalm 82:1-4. Ellicott notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate missed the sense, while the Syriac rendered it finely, “Be strong, and judge true judgment, and the Lord will be with you for ever” — and he cannot forbear observing that the king’s own name, Jehoshaphat, means “Jehovah judgeth,” so that the reformer of Judah’s courts bore the doctrine in his very name.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the double sense of God’s being “with” the judges: he is with them both to observe their carriage and to defend them against all those enemies whom the impartial exercise of justice is sure to provoke. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the motives into three, all taken from God: that from him the judges have their commission, being his ministers in a power ordained by him; that his eye is upon them, for he is with them in the judgment to call them to account if they do amiss; and that he is himself the great pattern of justice, in whom is no iniquity, no bribery, and no respect of persons — magistrates being called gods, and therefore bound to resemble him. The witnesses do not divide: to judge is to stand, for a fearful moment, in the room of God, and to answer to the God in whose room one stands.
7:
The charge is now clinched with a threefold description of the God whom the judges represent, and the witnesses read the verse as turning the doctrine of the last into a motive for holy fear. The reformed John Gill takes “let the fear of the LORD be upon you” to mean that the judges must act with that fear ever before their eyes and upon their hearts, a restraint that keeps the hand from wrong. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott parses the sentence with care: the opening “wherefore” is simply “and”; the “fear of the LORD” is a dread or awe of Jehovah, the same holy terror that had fallen upon the surrounding nations at 2 Chronicles 17:10; and “take heed and do it” is a hendiadys, a single charge to act heedfully and deal warily. The “iniquity” that is not found with God he defines precisely as a want of equity — unfairness, injustice — and he bids the reader add to the verse’s own catalogue the express prohibition against wresting judgment and taking a bribe at Deuteronomy 16:19. The principle he draws is exact: they who judge for Jehovah, as the previous verse had said, are bound to judge like Jehovah.

That last thought is the one the other witnesses seize. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states it plainly: you who are in God’s stead and do his work, and must one day give account of it to him, are therefore bound to imitate God herein — to be in your measure what he is without measure, just and impartial and incorruptible. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as grounding the fear of the LORD upon this very character of God, in whom there is no injustice, no partiality, and no taking of gifts; because he is such, his judges must be such, and the awe of him must sit upon every sentence they pass.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had already drawn out the same three disclaimers as the crowning motive of the charge: God is the great example of justice to all magistrates, in whom there is no iniquity, no bribery, nor respect of persons; and since magistrates are honoured with the name of gods, they must endeavour to resemble the God whose name they bear. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the fear upon the heart, Ellicott the equity upon the terms, and Wesley, Keil, and Henry the imitation upon the character of God — and all agree that the surest guard of a court is not the watching of men but the fear of a Judge who neither errs, nor favours, nor can be bought.
8:
The chapter now raises its second institution, the supreme court at the capital, and the witnesses attend both to its composition and to a knot in its closing words. The reformed John Gill describes it as the great court of judicature, made up of princes, priests, and Levites — of ecclesiastical and political persons together — because causes of both sorts were brought before it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as the tribunal to which the harder causes of the inferior courts were referred and appealed, sitting at Jerusalem under the eye of the king, and manned by Levites and priests most learned in the law together with the chief of the fathers of Israel, who were competent judges of matters of fact as the priests were of the sense of the law.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the measure in its legal history. The heads of the fathers’ houses had exercised judicial functions from Moses’ own ordinance at Exodus 18:21-26 and Deuteronomy 1:15-17; the six thousand Levites David had set apart as officers and judges at 1 Chronicles 23:4 served as their assessors, the professional experts in the Law; and Jehoshaphat, building on this, re-organised the whole administration and established in the capital just such a high court of appeal as the law had prescribed at Deuteronomy 17:8-12. He distinguishes the two kinds of cause the verse names — “the judgment of the LORD,” the ecclesiastical matters, and the “controversies” or civil litigation, the strife that the next mention will call “the king’s matters.”

Over the last clause the witnesses genuinely differ. The received text reads “when they returned to Jerusalem,” and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke doubts it. Who returned? he asks; and if the text meant that any person returned to Jerusalem, would it not have used the preposition, “to Jerusalem”? He judges, with learned men before him, that the word rendered “and they returned” should rather be pointed “the inhabitants,” so that the sense is “for the controversies of the inhabitants of Jerusalem” — a reading he finds preserved in the Vulgate’s “its inhabitants” and in the Septuagint’s “to judge the inhabitants of Jerusalem,” and parallel to a like slip at 2 Chronicles 34:9. Ellicott keeps the received consonants but ends the sentence at “controversies,” taking “and they returned to Jerusalem” as a fresh clause that looks back to the return of the royal commission of v.4; John Wesley reads it likewise of the moment when Jehoshaphat and his company came home to Jerusalem and there issued this ordinance. So the debate stands between emending the word to “inhabitants” and retaining “returned” as a note of time. Wesley adds a further open question the witnesses do not all answer alike — whether these officers formed a single court for all causes or two distinct benches, the one ecclesiastical and the other civil — a matter, he honestly grants, not easy to determine.
9:
Turning from the local benches to the high court, the king repeats his charge, and the witnesses note how deliberately the second commission echoes the first. The reformed John Gill marks simply that the charge is now addressed to the members of the court at Jerusalem. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws the parallel out: the word “thus” points forward to what the following verse will spell out, and the judges of the superior court are here charged exactly as the ordinary judges had been charged at vv.6-7 — to do their work in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart, that last phrase meaning integrity, the same soundness of heart praised in Asa at 2 Chronicles 15:17 and named in the eyes of the LORD that run to and fro at 2 Chronicles 16:9.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the same charge and to a nicety of its grammar. Jehoshaphat gave the members of the supreme tribunal orders to exercise their office in the fear of the Lord, with fidelity, and with an upright heart; the words “thus shall ye do” leave the content of the doing to be stated only in the verse that follows, and the little conjunction that opens that verse is explicative — “namely” — introducing the cases in which they are to act. The charge, in their reading, is not vague exhortation but the preface to a precise rule of procedure.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fastens on the inward spring of it all. The judges must see to it that they act from a good principle, doing all in the fear of the LORD, setting him always before them; and then, he says, they will act faithfully, conscientiously, and with a perfect upright heart. The witnesses do not divide, and their agreement is itself instructive. The same three notes sounded to the country judges are sounded again to the highest court in the land — the fear of God, fidelity, and integrity of heart — as if to say that no eminence of station alters the terms on which a man may judge his neighbour. Gill fixes the audience, Ellicott and Keil the wording and its forward reach, and Henry the principle beneath it; and all agree that the charge to the greatest bench is, at bottom, the charge to the least: to judge as before God, with clean hands and a whole heart.
10:
The high court’s jurisdiction is now defined, and the witnesses trace both the kinds of case it was to hear and the pastoral duty laid on it beyond the mere passing of sentence. The reformed John Gill takes the causes to be whatsoever, sacred or civil, came up by appeal from the inferior courts of the country where they could not be determined. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the opening “to wit,” and reads the whole as defining the appellate work of a supreme court: the causes come from “your brethren” — not the judges’ colleagues but their fellow-countrymen — who dwell in the country towns as opposed to the capital. “Between blood and blood,” a phrase drawn from the law of the hard cases at Deuteronomy 17:8, means the questions arising out of homicide, whether a given death were murder or manslaughter; “between law and commandment, statutes and judgments” gathers up the questions about the interpretation and application of the various legal rules.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same two heads — cases of manslaughter and accidental death, of consanguinity, inheritance, and family claims under the one, and whatever touched the moral precepts, the rites and ceremonies, or the civil affairs under the other. He is joined by the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and by John Wesley in a shared historical observation that explains why homicide in particular came up to Jerusalem: since the revolt of the ten tribes all the cities of refuge save Hebron had fallen to the northern kingdom, so that the manslayer of Judah now fled for sanctuary to the courts of the temple and the horns of the altar, and the trial of such cases was therefore reserved for the court in the capital.

On the clause “ye shall even warn them” the witnesses turn from procedure to conscience. Ellicott renders it “ye shall instruct them,” the verb meaning to teach, as at Exodus 18:20, the true sense and bearing of the law in the case at hand; to “trespass” is to incur guilt by giving false judgment, and the wrath that follows, the same wrath threatened at v.2, would fall not on the judges only but on the whole people, involving all in the guilt and its penalty. Wesley reads the warning as an admonition to the offender and to others to take better heed for the future, so that the court’s work is not only to sentence the past but to guard the days to come. Henry presses the sharpest point of all: “This do, and ye shall not trespass” implies that those who hold power in their hands contract the guilt of sin themselves if they do not use that power to prevent and restrain the sin of others — “you trespass if you do not keep them from trespassing.” The witnesses do not divide; together they make the bench a place of teaching as well as of doom, where a judge who fails to instruct is himself found guilty before the God for whom he judges.
11:
The chapter closes on the two heads of the supreme court and a final word of courage, and the witnesses read in the double presidency a wise division of the whole business of the realm. The reformed John Gill takes Amariah the chief priest to preside over the court in all things sacred, all that concerned the worship of God, being present to give his advice and to direct the determination of such causes according to the statutes provided for them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the structure out plainly: here was a two-fold jurisdiction, ecclesiastical and civil; in the ecclesiastical court Amariah the high priest was supreme judge, and in the civil Zebadiah was supreme, with the Levites serving both as a kind of counsellors. Without good and wholesome laws no nation can be prosperous, Clarke reflects, and vain are the best laws if they be not judiciously and conscientiously administered; and he lays down the principle the arrangement embodies — that the things of God and the things of the king should never be confounded, but Amariah the priest and Zebadiah the ruler should each keep his distinct place of jurisdiction.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms and refines the picture. “Amariah the chief priest” is rather the High Priest, the Head; and since in the priestly genealogy at 1 Chronicles 6:11 Amariah stands fifth from Zadok, and Jehoshaphat was the fifth king from David, the name probably denotes the very man then in office. Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, “the ruler of the house of Judah,” was the nagid or tribal prince, set as president over the civil causes, “all the king’s matters.” The clause about the Levites Ellicott renders literally, “and Writers shall the Levites be,” the inferior officials of the court, its scribes and notaries, acting in the judges’ presence and under their direction. The closing “deal courageously” he gives as “be strong and act,” a favourite locution of the chronicler’s, as at 1 Chronicles 28:10; and “the LORD shall be with the good” he reads as a wish or prayer — “Jehovah be with the good!” — another characteristic turn of the writer’s.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology of the arrangement. In the two presidents he sees diversities of gifts and operations, all from the same Spirit and all for the good of the body: some men best understand the matters of the LORD and others the king’s matters, and neither can say to the other, I have no need of thee, for God’s Israel has need of both. “Blessed be God,” Henry exclaims, “both for magistrates and ministers, scribes and statesmen, men of books and men of business.” And he hears in the final charge a call to resolution: deal courageously, and fear not the face of man; be bold in the discharge of duty, for whoever is against you, God will protect you — “the LORD shall be with the good.” Wherever he finds a good man and a good magistrate, Henry concludes, he will be found a good God. The witnesses do not divide; they leave the reformed courts of Judah standing under a promise, that the God who requires justice will himself be present with those who do it.
